explanations: terra: Seeking help through patience and prayer is described as weighty except for the humble, identifying a saving practice that itself feels difficult.
terra: The change of direction distinguishes one who follows the messenger from one who turns on his heels, using the source root's bodily retreat in a guidance test.
terra: Believers are commanded to seek help through patience and prayer and assured that God is with the patient, repeating the support named for the difficult crossing.

luna: The section’s day of hunger and fatigue, spent wealth, and counsel of patience meet in this test of “الْجُوعِ ... وَنَقْصٍ مِّنَ الْأَمْوَالِ”; hardship names concrete conditions, not an abstract obstacle. | terra: Fear, hunger, and losses test the travelers, while the ayah commands good news for the patient; hunger-with-hardship and endurance are concrete features of the section.

luna: Following the hunger and wealth-loss trial in 2:155, this ayah gives the response “إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّا إِلَيْهِ رَاجِعُونَ,” a way of holding steady through affliction. | terra: The tested people of 2:155 hold their direction under affliction by locating both origin and return with God.

luna: This completes the trial-and-response sequence after 2:155–156: God’s blessing, mercy, and the description “هُمُ الْمُهْتَدُونَ” connect patient endurance to guidance. | terra: Those who endure the test receive mercy and are explicitly called the guided, linking patience under hardship to successful guidance.

luna: The section turns the pass toward feeding hungry people; here those who conceal revelation “يَأْكُلُونَ فِي بُطُونِهِمْ إِلَّا النَّارَ,” a reversal in which eating ends in Fire. | terra: Those who conceal scripture for a small price consume only fire, turning withheld guidance and purchased wealth into inward fire.

luna: The section cites the secondary sense of ص ب ر as daring, not steadfast restraint; “فَمَا أَصْبَرَهُمْ عَلَى النَّارِ” turns that capacity toward the Fire after the preceding ayah’s warning. | terra: They exchange guidance for error and are described as astonishingly enduring toward fire, the section's explicit reversal of saving patience.

luna: This ayah gathers the section’s concrete moral route into one account: freeing people, giving to kin, orphan, and needy, then “الصَّابِرِينَ فِي الْبَأْسَاءِ وَالضَّرَّاءِ.” | terra: True righteousness includes giving cherished wealth, freeing people, and patience in poverty, suffering, and danger—the same costly acts and endurance that constitute the pass.
luna: Alongside the section’s food on a day of hunger, this fasting ayah names “فِدْيَةٌ طَعَامُ مِسْكِينٍ,” a concrete obligation to feed a needy person in the setting of abstention and capacity.
terra: God intends ease rather than hardship in the fasting ordinance, guarding the difficult-road image from implying that hardship is desired for itself.

luna: The section’s dictionary account of ق ح م includes throwing oneself into a severe situation; in the context of spending and doing good, this ayah warns “وَلَا تُلْقُوا بِأَيْدِيكُمْ إِلَى التَّهْلُكَةِ,” setting a boundary between the moral climb and reckless self-destruction. | terra: The command to spend on God's road is paired with a prohibition against throwing oneself into destruction, marking the boundary between courageous expenditure and blind self-ruin.

luna: The section says hardship is already human ground and the climb must be entered willingly; this asks whether people think they will enter the Garden before affliction and shaking have come. | terra: The believers are asked whether they expect to enter the Garden without the severe distress and shaking suffered by earlier travelers; the destination lies beyond lived hardship.
terra: Right direction has become distinct from error, and choosing it is pictured as taking hold of an unbreakable handhold; disclosure must be followed by bodily commitment.

luna: The section distinguishes wealth poured away from effort that relieves hunger; this gives the contrasting image of spending for God’s cause as a seed multiplied many times over. | terra: Wealth spent in God's road grows like a seed into many ears, reversing the boast that expenditure simply annihilates piled wealth.
terra: Those who spend for God's pleasure and inner firmness are compared to a garden on raised ground, bringing expenditure and literal elevation into one image.
terra: Satan's promise of poverty explains how fear blocks expenditure, while God's promise of forgiveness and bounty discloses the other end.
terra: Open charity is good and hidden giving to the poor is better, directly repeating the public-and-secret expenditure joined to patience in 13:22.
terra: The ayah distinguishes God's act of guidance from the believer's act of spending and says that good expenditure returns to the giver who seeks God's face.
terra: The deserving poor are constrained in God's road and unable to travel the earth, joining bodily restriction and hidden need to the giver's obligation.
terra: Those who spend by night and day, secretly and openly, enact the expenditure cited beside patience and عُقْبَى ٱلدَّارِ in 13:22.

luna: The section stresses real hardship while describing a demanded moral ascent; this closing prayer supplies a capacity boundary: “لَا يُكَلِّفُ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا,” so the difficult path is not an impossible burden. | terra: God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity, setting a limit around the section's claim that the pass demands real exertion.
terra: The good is not reached until one spends what one loves, making expenditure the costly threshold to be crossed.
terra: The community had stood on the lip of a pit of fire and God rescued it, supplying the precipice beside the route and the opposite of falling into it.
terra: The command to travel through the earth and inspect the deniers' outcome makes عاقبة a road's observable end in the source section's secondary sense.

luna: The section asks for a deliberate climb rather than imagining the destination without passage; this asks whether people expect to enter the Garden before God makes evident those who strive and remain patient. | terra: The question whether believers expect to enter the Garden before striving and patience are manifested directly denies arrival without the difficult crossing.
terra: The question whether believers will turn back on their heels if the messenger dies turns spiritual retreat into the exact bodily motion developed beside the pass.
terra: Believers are warned that obeying the disbelievers will turn them back on their heels and return them as losers.
terra: Those who withhold God's bounty wrongly think it good; what they withheld will be collared around them on the final day.
terra: Testing in wealth and persons is paired with patience and taqwa as matters of resolve, connecting expenditure, hardship, and endurance.
terra: The layered command to be patient, outlast others, and remain stationed gives patience the bodily firmness required in a frightening passage.
terra: God wishes to lighten the human burden because the human was created weak, bounding chosen exertion by creaturely capacity.
terra: The miserly both withhold and command others to withhold while concealing God's bounty, reversing the travelers' mutual counsel toward generosity.
terra: Those who sit back without disability are distinguished from those who strive with wealth and body, closely matching the contrast between immobility and undertaking the difficult act.
terra: The migrant finds many refuges and spaciousness on the road, and even death after setting out leaves his reward secured with God.
terra: Opposing the messenger after guidance is clear and following a road other than the believers' road is a direct, if abstract, version of choosing the other visible route.
terra: Disbelief and obstruction of God's road are themselves described as straying far, turning the blockers into lost travelers.
terra: Moses commands his people to enter the assigned land and not turn back on their rear sides lest they become losers.
terra: The people cite the land's formidable inhabitants and refuse entry until the obstacle removes itself, a direct refusal before a difficult crossing.
terra: Two God-fearing men tell them to enter through the gate and promise that committed entry will bring victory.
terra: The people answer that Moses and his Lord should fight while they remain sitting, making bodily non-action explicit.
terra: Their refused entry ends in forty years of forbidden arrival and wandering through the land, an aimless hardship produced by avoiding the purposeful one.
terra: Travel through the earth is again ordered so the deniers' outcome may be seen, concretizing result as the terminus of a journey.

luna: The section labels as a secondary dictionary sense of ع ق ب turning back on one’s heels; this ayah says “نَرُدُّ عَلَىٰ أَعْقَابِنَا بَعْدَ إِذْ هَدَانَا اللَّهُ,” making retreat after guidance the precise opposite of entering the pass. | terra: The person turned back on his heels after God's guidance wanders bewildered while companions call him toward guidance; heel-turning, perplexity, and the offered road meet in one scene.

luna: The section says the route is placed before the person; “قَدْ جَاءَكُم بَصَائِرُ مِن رَّبِّكُمْ” and the ensuing seeing/blindness distinction make sight and responsibility after evidence explicit.

luna: The section describes an uphill exertion and a body that must enter difficulty; here a tight chest is likened to “يَصَّعَّدُ فِي السَّمَاءِ,” within an ayah explicitly contrasting divine guidance and misguidance. | terra: Misguidance is pictured as a constricted chest like someone painfully climbing into the sky, a direct bodily image of ascent, distress, and guidance.
terra: The warning that people will learn who possesses the outcome of the abode makes recompense the final ownership of a route, though no physical road is staged.

luna: The section’s two ridges become a choice after the way is shown; this ayah commands “هَٰذَا صِرَاطِي مُسْتَقِيمًا” and warns that other paths scatter people from it. | terra: God identifies His straight road and commands people to follow it rather than the other roads that divide them away from it.
terra: Those who threaten from every road and divert people from God's way are told to inspect the corrupters' outcome, joining road obstruction to road-end.
terra: Moses tells his people to seek God's help and be patient, then declares that the earth's final outcome belongs to the wary.
terra: The arrogant see the way of right and do not take it, but see the way of error and take it; visibility, two routes, and refusal all coincide with the image.
terra: God could have raised the sign-bearer, but he clung to the earth and followed desire; chosen low attachment replaces possible elevation.
terra: People possess eyes but do not see with them and are called farther astray, supporting the distinction between furnished perception and actual guidance.
terra: The disbelievers spend wealth to block God's road, then their spending becomes regret and ends in defeat and gathering to Hell; expenditure, obstruction, and outcome form one chain.
terra: At a terrifying encounter believers are told to stand firm and remember God, staging the self-possession that the section derives from patience.
terra: The command not to quarrel and lose courage ends with patient endurance, showing how the travelers preserve strength while under pressure.
terra: Satan turns back on his heels after seeing what the opposing army cannot see; the exact retreat motion appears here in a different, fearful context.
terra: The Prophet must urge believers into the hard encounter, and patient endurance is said to overcome far greater numbers.
terra: God lightens the combat burden because of human weakness while still naming patient endurance, setting a measured limit around demanded toughness.
terra: Believers are asked whether they expect to be left without their striving and loyalties being made known, another denial of untested arrival.
terra: Family, accumulated wealth, trade, and homes are set against striving with wealth and body; attachment to possessions can stop the traveler.
terra: Hoarded gold and silver and failure to spend on God's road receive a warning of painful punishment.
terra: The hoarded treasure is heated in Hell and used to brand its owners, making withheld wealth return bodily as fire.
terra: When told to set out, some cling heavily to the earth and prefer near life, a bodily refusal to rise and move.
terra: Those who refuse to set out are threatened with painful punishment and replacement, giving the earth-clinging refusal of 9:38 its end.
terra: The command to set out light or heavy and strive with wealth and selves supplies both bodily advance and costly expenditure.
terra: An easy gain and short journey would have drawn the laggards, but the long distance deterred them, exposing refusal that appears specifically when the road is hard.
terra: Those left behind rejoice at sitting, dislike exertion with wealth and body, and cite the heat; the answer that Hell is hotter makes avoided strain return as fire.
terra: Affluent men ask permission to remain with those who sit when commanded to believe and strive, giving the lagging image a social form.
terra: Their contentment with those left behind fixes the refusal of 9:86 as chosen immobility rather than inability.
terra: The weak, sick, and those lacking means are exempt when sincere, marking bodily inability as a real boundary distinct from willful refusal.
terra: Those who cannot find mounts turn back weeping because they lack means, a compassionate reversal of heel-turning through reluctance.
terra: Blame falls on wealthy people who ask leave to remain behind, tying capacity and possessions to refused advance.
terra: A foundation on the edge of a collapsing cliff gives way with its builder into Hellfire, making moral construction terminate in a literal downward plunge.
terra: Believers exchange their lives and wealth for the Garden, making bodily risk and expenditure the price of the reached abode.
terra: God does not let a guided people stray until He has clarified what they must avoid, supporting the section's insistence on disclosure before culpable failure.
terra: Refusing to lag behind is explained through thirst, fatigue, and hunger suffered on God's road, the same bodily cost gathered around ascent and masghaba.
terra: Every expenditure and every valley crossed is credited, uniting spent wealth with actual passage through difficult terrain.
terra: The ayah asks whether the one who guides to truth is more worthy to be followed than one who cannot guide without first being guided.
terra: Wrongdoers obstruct God's road and seek it crooked while denying the Hereafter, linking route obstruction to denial of its end.
terra: No mountain can shelter Noah's son from God's decree; physical height cannot replace entering the offered means of rescue.
terra: Noah is commanded to be patient and is promised that the outcome belongs to the wary, pairing endurance on the way with its end.
terra: Pharaoh goes before his people on Judgment Day and leads them into fire, an exact dark reversal of the guide named for preceding those he guides.

luna: The section explicitly names root ع ق ب for an end or recompense and sets it beside patience and spending; this ayah joins both acts to “عُقْبَى الدَّارِ,” the final outcome of the abode. | terra: Patience for the Lord's face, prayer, and spending secretly and openly culminate in عُقْبَى ٱلدَّارِ, joining endurance and expenditure to the road's good end.

luna: After 13:22 names “عُقْبَى الدَّارِ,” this adjacent ayah makes that outcome concrete as gardens entered with righteous family; it contributes the destination beyond the pass. | terra: Gardens and the entry of the righteous family supply the reached abode whose outcome 13:22 names and whose gates the angels enter.

luna: The section links patient passage through hardship to its end; the greeting “بِمَا صَبَرْتُمْ” culminates in “فَنِعْمَ عُقْبَى الدَّارِ,” the same root-family outcome. | terra: The angels connect peace and the excellent عُقْبَى ٱلدَّارِ expressly to the travelers' patience.
terra: Those who break covenant, sever what God commands joined, and corrupt the earth receive the curse and the bad abode, the opposed continuation to 13:22-24.
terra: The ayah names the two ends with the source section's root: the outcome of the wary is the Garden, while the outcome of the disbelievers is fire.
terra: The disbelievers will learn who possesses the outcome of the abode, repeating the section's use of عُقْبَى for the final owner of the road's end.
terra: Those who prefer near life bar people from God's road and seek to make it crooked, combining wrong preference with active deformation of the route.
terra: Lot's ruined settlement remains on an established road, making past destruction a visible sign encountered by later travelers.

luna: The section’s image is of alternatives already shown; this ayah says “قَصْدُ السَّبِيلِ” belongs to God while some ways turn aside, giving a direct straight/deviant-path boundary. | terra: God assumes responsibility for directing the road while acknowledging that some roads deviate, a close counterpart to guidance that places distinct routes before the traveler.
terra: Mountains, rivers, and roads are placed in the earth so people can find their way, joining raised land to traversable routes.
terra: Landmarks and stars complete 16:15's road scene by furnishing visible means through which travelers are guided.
terra: After messengers call every community to serve God and avoid false gods, travel reveals the deniers' outcome, joining disclosed alternatives and their end.
terra: Those who disbelieve and obstruct God's road receive added punishment for their corruption, supplying the obstruction's destination.
terra: A secure, well-provisioned town that rejects God's gifts is made to taste hunger and fear, reversing provision into the hardship its ingratitude denied.
terra: Patience is located in God's aid, while grief and constriction over opponents are forbidden, directly answering the bodily distress gathered around the climb.
luna: Against boasting of wealth without taking the difficult way, this describes one who desires the Hereafter and “سَعَىٰ لَهَا سَعْيَهَا”; the effort of that believer is accepted.

luna: The section presents wealth put to effort for hungry and needy people; “وَآتِ ذَا الْقُرْبَىٰ حَقَّهُ” directs resources toward relatives and the vulnerable rather than boastful disposal. | terra: Giving relatives, the poor, and the traveler their due specifies where wealth must move rather than be held or wasted.
luna: The section names root ه ل ك in the boast “I consumed heaps of wealth”; this ayah’s “وَلَا تُبَذِّرْ تَبْذِيرًا” directly marks wasteful spending as the contrary course.
terra: The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor opened without limit, giving bodily form to the boundary between miserliness and ruinous expenditure.

luna: The section’s root ن ج د carries elevation and height; this ayah warns against walking proudly and says a person will not reach the mountains in height, setting a limit on arrogant claims of mastery over the terrain.
terra: One blind in this life is still blinder in the Hereafter and farther astray from the road, connecting unused perception to failed direction.
terra: The command to hold oneself with those who call on their Lord enacts the source definition of patience as restraining the self rather than fleeing discomfort.
terra: Truth is disclosed, belief or disbelief is left as a choice, and the disbeliever's fire is already described, joining shown alternatives to destination.

luna: The section hears the boast of spent wealth as wealth falling into a gap; this garden owner watches his produce destroyed and turns his hands over what he had spent, making loss and regret visible. | terra: The ruined owner turns his palms over what he spent while his garden lies fallen on its trellises, joining expenditure, destruction, and downward collapse.
luna: The section explicitly names ع ق ب for the end and recompense; after the garden’s ruin, this ayah says God is “خَيْرٌ عُقْبًا,” locating the true final outcome beyond worldly property.

luna: After the ruined garden in 18:42, this ayah compares worldly life to water after which vegetation dries and becomes wind-scattered stubble; it extends the section’s image of wealth and effort falling away.

luna: The section names ع ق ب as the end and distinguishes a difficult moral route from wasted wealth; this ayah contrasts worldly wealth and children with “الْبَاقِيَاتُ الصَّالِحَاتُ” that are better in reward and hope.

luna: The section says مسغبة is hunger joined to fatigue; on a journey, Moses asks for food and says “لَقَدْ لَقِينَا مِن سَفَرِنَا هَٰذَا نَصَبًا,” joining a meal to travel-weariness. | terra: Moses names bodily fatigue from the journey; it specifically echoes the section's exhausted traveler, though this journey is not itself the moral pass.

luna: The section gives ع ق ب the secondary sense of turning back on one’s heels; after the journey-fatigue in 18:62, Moses and his companion retrace their route: “فَارْتَدَّا عَلَىٰ آثَارِهِمَا قَصَصًا.” | terra: Moses and his servant deliberately retrace their footsteps to recover the sought place; turning back on a route here repairs an omission rather than abandons guidance.
terra: Abraham asks his father to follow him so that he may guide him on an even road, closely matching the guide who advances before the traveler.

terra: Moses identifies his staff as something he leans on and uses in other ways; it faintly anchors the source dictionary's guiding staff in a Quranic object, though this ayah does not say it probes the road.
terra: Moses describes the Lord as the One who gave each thing its created form and then guided it, a general formulation of creation followed by direction.
terra: God commands Moses to lead the servants by night and strike out a dry road through the sea without fear, joining advance, staff-mediated passage, and reassurance.
terra: At the descent to earthly life God promises that whoever follows His guidance will neither stray nor suffer, making response to prior guidance decisive.
terra: Turning away from the reminder produces a constricted life and blind resurrection, the ruinous result of refusing the shown way.
terra: The resurrected person asks why he is blind although he had been able to see, foregrounding the difference between incapacity and culpable refusal.
terra: God answers that signs came and were abandoned, confirming that the person's blindness follows neglect of what had been shown.
terra: Perseverance in prayer, God's provision, and the statement that the outcome belongs to taqwa gather patient exertion, sustenance, and the road's end.
terra: Firm mountains contain broad passes as roads so that people may be guided; this supplies the literal mountain-road anatomy developed for the pass.
terra: God makes exemplary people leaders who guide by His command and perform good works, another positive form of the guide who goes before.
terra: One who worships on an edge turns away when trial strikes, combining precarious terrain, testing, and retreat.
terra: Every attempted escape from the fire's anguish sends its people back into it, a punitive reversal of passing through hardship to freedom.
luna: The section makes a mountain pass the physical scene of a demanded crossing; here pilgrims answer the call by coming “مِن كُلِّ فَجٍّ عَمِيقٍ,” traversing far, deep passes toward the House.
terra: Associating partners with God is likened to falling from the sky and being snatched or cast far away, supplying the downward opposite of the saving ascent.
terra: Travel through the earth should produce understanding hearts and hearing ears; the ayah insists that the decisive blindness is inward, not lack of physical eyes.
terra: The command to strive fully is paired with the assurance that no constriction has been placed in religion, bounding moral difficulty against pointless impossibility.

terra: Mary and Jesus are lodged on elevated, settled ground with flowing water; the literal raised terrain and provision are specific, but their relation to the difficult two-ridge choice is indirect.

luna: A branch of the section’s root ب ل د describes a horse left behind the front-runners; this ayah pictures believers “يُسَارِعُونَ فِي الْخَيْرَاتِ” and “سَابِقُونَ,” the active opposite of lagging at the pass.
terra: People who heard God's signs are described as recoiling on their heels, making retreat follow disclosed speech rather than ignorance.
terra: Owners are commanded to contract for emancipation when good is known in the enslaved and to give them from God's wealth, concretely joining freeing to expenditure.
terra: The messenger asks no payment, only that whoever wills take a road toward his Lord.
terra: Moses' staff opens the sea and leaves each parted side like a tremendous mountain, forming a traversable corridor between two raised walls.
terra: Travel and inspection of the criminals' outcome turn the source root's abstract recompense back into a route and its terminus.
terra: As Moses physically turns toward Midian, he hopes that his Lord will guide him to the even road, joining actual travel and divine guidance.
terra: Leaders who call people toward fire reverse the good guide's forward position and reveal where false leadership ends.
terra: Qarun attributes his wealth to his own knowledge but is reminded that God destroyed people stronger and more numerous than he.
terra: The earth swallows Qarun and his house, giving arrogant wealth an emphatic downward end with no helpers.
terra: Those who had desired his position recognize that provision is expanded or constrained by God and that deniers do not succeed.

luna: The section’s dictionary family ن ج د begins with height, while ع ق ب names the final outcome; this ayah joins refusal of “عُلُوًّا فِي الْأَرْضِ” to the statement that the good outcome belongs to the mindful. | terra: The final abode is for those who seek neither elevation nor corruption on earth, and the outcome belongs to the wary; worldly height is bounded by the true end.
terra: People are not left merely to say they believe without being tested, denying arrival by verbal claim alone.
terra: Testing earlier peoples distinguishes truthful travelers from liars, giving the hardship in 29:2 its revelatory purpose.

luna: The section says guidance has already been shown and the missing act is striving; God says of those who strive, “لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا,” joining exertion to being guided on paths. | terra: Those who exert themselves for God are promised guidance into His ways, joining deliberate effort to further guidance rather than treating guidance as a substitute for effort.
terra: Travel reveals earlier peoples of greater strength, cultivation, and building who nevertheless wronged themselves after messengers brought signs.
terra: Giving the relative, poor person, and traveler their due is called better for those who seek God's face, echoing both the pass's recipients and Godward intent.
terra: The listener must travel through the earth and see the earlier associators' outcome, a repeated Quranic enactment of road-to-end.
terra: After commanding active moral work, Luqman tells his son to endure what befalls him and calls this a matter requiring resolve.
terra: Whenever the wrongdoers try to leave the fire, they are returned to it, turning avoidance of the saving difficulty into a destination with no exit.
terra: Leaders guide by God's command when they exercise patience and certainty, joining the guide who goes before with the endurance required on the way.
terra: In encirclement, eyes swerve and hearts reach throats, supplying the bodily panic from which patience must hold the self.
terra: Believers are tested and violently shaken in that position, a concrete instance of entering the middle of frightening hardship.
terra: The condemned say their masters and great ones led them away from the road, showing guidance's social form turned into misdirection.
terra: Visible settlements and measured stages make a safe journey possible, presenting a route whose provision and distances have already been arranged.
terra: The people ask that their journeys be lengthened and thereby wrong themselves, turning a furnished road into dispersal and ruin.
terra: Good words ascend to God and righteous action raises them, giving moral work a vertical movement that complements the bodily ascent of the pass.
terra: Travel reveals the outcome of people stronger than the present deniers, placing physical strength under the judgment of the road's end.
terra: A man runs from the far end of the city and urges his people to follow the messengers, embodying urgent forward response to guidance.
terra: He commands them to follow guides who ask no payment and are themselves guided, clarifying whom the running man follows.
terra: When commanded to spend from God's provision, the disbelievers refuse to feed those in need, a spoken rejection of the disclosed deed.
terra: The command not to serve Satan identifies one allegiance as an enemy-led course.
terra: The command to serve God names that worship as a straight road, completing the two-allegiance scene of 36:60.
terra: The command to guide the wrongdoers onto the road of Hell uses guidance and a road for the punitive opposite destination.
terra: Travelers pass the destroyed people of Lot in the morning, placing the warning directly on their ordinary route.
terra: They pass the same ruins at night yet are asked whether they will understand, showing repeated visibility without moral response.
terra: The transgressors are assigned an evil place of return, introducing the destination that 38:56 names and the plunging crowd of 38:59 enters.
terra: Hell is the evil resting place into which the damned enter, supplying the destination for the plunging crowd of 38:59.

luna: The section says the person did not “iqtahama” the pass; “مُّقْتَحِمٌ مَّعَكُمْ” uses the same root for a crowd plunging into the Fire, reversing the refused ascent into an assault on ruin. | terra: A crowd plunges into the fire with its leaders using the other Quranic form of the section's اقتحم root; the unmade plunge at the saving pass becomes a plunge into punishment.
terra: Travel shows the outcome of earlier peoples whose greater power and earthly traces did not save them.
terra: Pharaoh claims that he guides his people only to the way of right; 40:38 later exposes the same formula in the mouth of the true believing guide.
terra: The believing man asks his people to follow him so he may guide them to the way of right, explicitly putting a guide in front of travelers.
terra: He contrasts the passing enjoyment of the nearer life with the lasting abode of the Hereafter, explaining the destination of his offered way.
terra: The journey to former peoples' outcome shows that numbers, strength, traces, and earnings could not avail them, answering the source's confidence in wealth and power.

luna: The section says the person cannot excuse refusal as an unseen route; of Thamud, “فَهَدَيْنَاهُمْ فَاسْتَحَبُّوا الْعَمَىٰ عَلَى الْهُدَىٰ” makes rejection after guidance explicit. | terra: Thamud were guided but preferred blindness to guidance, making culpable preference rather than inability to find the road the decisive failure.
terra: The messenger is told that revelation enables him to guide people toward a straight road, placing a human guide before the travelers.
terra: The next ayah identifies that straight road as God's road and places the whole journey under God's final return.
terra: God makes the earth traversable and places roads in it so people may be guided, another literal road furnished before travel.
terra: Turning blind from the reminder is answered by a satanic companion, showing a case where neglected guidance produces deceptive accompaniment.
terra: Those companions avert people from the road while the people think themselves guided, a boundary case against the section's fully visible refusal.
terra: The messenger is commanded to hold fast to revelation because he is upon a straight road, joining firmness of grip to correct direction.
terra: The messenger is commanded to endure like the resolute messengers and not hasten the deniers' end, joining patience to confidence in the coming destination.
terra: God lets the works of those who disbelieve and obstruct His road go astray, making their attempted road-block rebound upon their own deeds.
terra: Travel discloses the end of earlier peoples whom God destroyed, linking the road's عاقبة to the destruction sense developed beside it.
terra: Those who turn back after guidance has become clear enact the section's heel-turn after a route has been shown.
terra: God's testing makes the strivers and the patient manifest, joining difficult action to the endurance that sustains it.
terra: Disbelief, obstruction of God's road, and opposition after guidance has become clear again make post-guidance resistance the issue.
terra: People are called to spend, yet some are miserly; the ayah says their refusal harms themselves, directly staging the call and non-action at the pass.
terra: Those left behind claim that wealth and families occupied them, making worldly holdings the stated reason the body did not advance.
terra: The laggards who avoided the earlier expedition ask to follow once spoils are available, exposing selective willingness when the difficult road becomes profitable.
terra: The former laggards are called toward a formidable people and given reward for obedience or punishment for another turn away, renewing the test of advance.
terra: Blindness, lameness, and sickness remove blame, again separating inability to travel from refusal after the route is known.
terra: The righteous recognize in their wealth a right for the asker and the deprived, repeating the distribution that reverses withholding.
terra: Guidance has come from the Lord, yet people follow conjecture and desire, another instance of preference overriding supplied direction.

luna: The section makes strenuous, chosen passage central to the moral road; “وَأَن لَّيْسَ لِلْإِنسَانِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَىٰ” states that a person’s own striving is what counts. | terra: The human has only what he strives for, so the road's result belongs to enacted exertion rather than merely seeing the route.

luna: Following the claim in 53:39, this ayah says “وَأَنَّ سَعْيَهُ سَوْفَ يُرَىٰ”; it adds that the person’s striving will be seen, fitting the section’s insistence that the path is exposed and action is accountable. | terra: A person's striving will be seen, echoing the section's insistence that the decisive missing thing is the bodily act.

luna: This completes the striving passage after 53:39–40: “ثُمَّ يُجْزَاهُ الْجَزَاءَ الْأَوْفَىٰ” gives the full recompense that corresponds to the section’s root-family link between the pass and its final outcome. | terra: The fullest recompense for striving supplies the road's final return after the effort of 53:39-40.
terra: Humans and jinn are challenged to pass beyond the regions of heaven and earth but told they cannot penetrate without authority, illuminating the source's language of passage and no exit.
terra: The companions of the right are named as one final group, repeating the two-sided human outcome that stands after the pass.
terra: The companions of the left are named as the opposed final group.
terra: Those who spent and struggled before victory receive a higher degree than later actors, joining timely expenditure to moral elevation.
terra: A good loan to God is promised multiplication and noble reward, another reversal of wealth as merely consumed or lost.
terra: The Helpers prefer others even while in privation, showing the pass's feeding and spending as an act undertaken from within one's own hardship.
terra: The final outcome of Satan and the person he misleads is that both remain in fire, pairing a false caller with the road's disastrous عاقبة.
terra: A saving transaction is announced, framing the next ayah's costly action as a route out of painful punishment.
terra: Faith and striving with wealth and body are the saving transaction, combining material expenditure and personal exertion.
terra: Forgiveness and gardens are the reached return of that expenditure and effort.
terra: People are told to spend before death arrives and makes the refuser wish for delay so that he could give charity and become righteous.
terra: Wealth and children are called a test while the great reward remains with God, placing possessions within the road's trial rather than outside it.
terra: The command to fear God as far as one can, listen, obey, and spend joins bodily capacity, forward response, and victory over miserliness.
terra: For the person who exercises taqwa, God makes an exit, directly answering the section's image of a difficulty through which a way must be found.
terra: Unexpected provision, divine sufficiency, and a measure fixed for everything supply what the traveler cannot see in advance.
terra: Both the affluent and the constrained must spend from what God gave; limited burden is followed by God's promise to make ease after hardship.
terra: Rebellious settlements taste the consequence of their conduct, and the عاقبة of their affair is loss, using the road-end root for collective ruin.
terra: Humans are told to walk the earth's shoulders, eat God's provision, and remember the resurrection to Him, joining raised terrain, sustenance, travel, and end.
terra: The ayah contrasts one walking fallen on his face with one walking upright on a straight road, turning moral guidance into bodily posture and movement.
terra: The garden owners explicitly resolve that no poor person will enter their crop that day, staging deliberate withholding of food.
terra: After the garden's destruction, the owners recognize that they themselves have been deprived, making withheld provision return as deprivation.
terra: Receiving the record in the right hand opens the fortunate branch of the same passage that later exposes useless wealth and neglected feeding.
terra: Receiving the record in the left hand opens the branch whose owner will confess that wealth failed and the poor were not fed.
terra: The condemned person's wealth has not benefited him, answering the boast about consumed wealth with its uselessness at the journey's end.
terra: His authority has perished, placing the source root's destruction sense beside the collapse of worldly power.
terra: The failed person is seized and bound, beginning the compulsory bodily movement toward punishment.
terra: He is thrust into Hellfire, giving the non-feeder's course a physical destination.
terra: He is then inserted into a long chain, intensifying the contrast between saving self-restraint and punitive confinement.
terra: Failure to urge feeding the poor is named among the causes of this ruined end.

luna: The section defines patience as holding the self back from panic; “خُلِقَ هَلُوعًا” names the contrasting human disposition the climb must resist. | terra: The human is created anxious, providing the native condition from which patience must restrain the self.

luna: The section contrasts steadiness on the pass with panic; this ayah specifies that the person is “إِذَا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعًا,” crying out when harm touches him. | terra: When harm touches him he panics, precisely the جَزُوعًا response named in the section's definition of patience.
terra: When good touches him he withholds, pairing panic before hardship with refusal to expend what the pass requires.
terra: Those devoted to prayer are excepted from the panic-and-withholding pattern, opening the alternative course.
terra: Constancy in prayer gives the alternative course the sustained discipline of a traveler who does not turn back.
terra: The successful group recognizes a fixed right within its wealth, reversing possessive withholding.
terra: That right belongs to the asker and the deprived, identifying the people whom expenditure must reach.
terra: Broad mountain roads across the spread earth may faintly illuminate the source's rugged pass by contrast; the ayah concerns ordinary travel, so the moral bridge remains uncertain.
terra: Whoever turns from the Lord's reminder is made to tread an ascending punishment, reversing refusal of the shown hard way into a compulsory hard ascent.
terra: The warning is a reminder from which whoever wills may take a road toward the Lord.
terra: God recognizes bodily limits, illness, travel, and struggle, then lightens the imposed exertion while retaining prayer and expenditure.
terra: The man assigned the forced ascent of 74:17 had first been given extensive wealth, matching the section's wealthy refuser.
terra: God had smoothed life out for him, sharpening the irony that his refusal will culminate in a forced hard climb.
terra: His demand for still more exposes appetite for increase rather than expenditure on the difficult good.
terra: His stubborn opposition to God's signs identifies why the man of ease and wealth is assigned the ascent in 74:17.

luna: The section’s pass is a hard ascent one must choose to enter; after 74:11–16 introduces a richly endowed denier, this ayah makes his ascent forced: “سَأُرْهِقُهُ صَعُودًا.” | terra: The wealthy sign-denier is forced into صَعُودًا, an arduous ascent; the climb he would not choose as moral action returns as imposed punishment.
terra: The question of what brought the guilty into Saqar frames fire as the reached destination of a sequence of refusals.
terra: The guilty confess that they did not feed the poor, explicitly carrying failure at the pass into the fire scene.

luna: This ayah supplies the setting for 76:3’s shown road: humanity is created from a mixed drop “نَّبْتَلِيهِ,” so the choice of route occurs within a trial. | terra: God creates the human from a mixed drop in order to test him, supplying the creation-and-trial premise immediately before the shown road of 76:3.

luna: The section names the root ه د ي (“to guide”) and insists the ridges are visible before the choice; here “هَدَيْنَاهُ السَّبِيلَ” is followed by grateful or ungrateful travelers, so failure lies in response to a shown way. | terra: After creating the human for trial, God says He showed him the road, then names its two responses, gratitude and disbelief; this is the closest parallel to the two visible ridges.

luna: The section’s path leads to feeding the hungry, orphan, and poor; this ayah directly stages feeding “مِسْكِينًا وَيَتِيمًا وَأَسِيرًا,” adding the captive to that concrete charitable route. | terra: Feeding the poor person, orphan, and captive despite love of the food closely restages the concrete deeds on the far side of the pass.

luna: After the feeding act in 76:8, this ayah says they feed only for God’s sake and seek neither repayment nor thanks; it distinguishes costly aid from the boast of having spent much. | terra: The feeders seek neither repayment nor thanks, locating the difficult act in its Godward intention.

luna: This continues the motive in 76:9: those who feed fear a grim day, linking the section’s hard, present act to its final reckoning. | terra: Their fear of a grim, distressful day explains why present generosity is the meaningful difficult road rather than avoidance of all difficulty.

luna: After the fear in 76:10, this ayah says God protects them from that day’s evil; it supplies the divine response to the section’s patient passage through hardship. | terra: God protects the feeders from that day's evil and grants radiance and joy, supplying the result of their chosen act.

luna: This completes the feeding-and-recompense sequence: “وَجَزَاهُم بِمَا صَبَرُوا جَنَّةً” explicitly joins patience to the Garden, the outcome beyond the section’s climb. | terra: The Garden is explicitly their reward for patience, joining the completed acts of feeding to endurance and outcome.
terra: The reminder is offered so that whoever wills may take a road to the Lord, stating the voluntary road image directly.
terra: Human willing is placed within God's will, supplying the theological boundary around the choice in 76:29.
terra: Mercy for whom God wills and painful punishment for wrongdoers give the chosen road its two ends.
terra: The true Day is announced and the listener is invited to take a place of return toward the Lord, joining route and final return.
terra: Transgression marks the first of two opposed human courses.
terra: Preferring the nearer life identifies the choice that makes the easy-looking course end badly.
terra: Hell is the abode of that first course, giving it a terminal destination.

luna: The section defines patience as holding the self back from panic; “وَنَهَى النَّفْسَ عَنِ الْهَوَىٰ” describes deliberate restraint of the self, joined here to fear of standing before the Lord. | terra: The second person fears standing before the Lord and restrains the self from desire, enacting patience as self-restraint.

luna: This completes 79:40’s self-restraint with its stated destination: “فَإِنَّ الْجَنَّةَ هِيَ الْمَأْوَىٰ,” an end reached by resisting desire. | terra: The Garden is the abode reached by the self-restraining course.
terra: God creates the human and makes the way easy; if السَّبِيل refers to birth or life's course, it supplies a deliberate counterpoint to the later chosen hard crossing.
terra: The reminder addresses whoever wills to go straight, turning response into an act of directed movement.
terra: The next ayah locates that willing within the will of God, bounding the traveler's choice without erasing it.

luna: This is a nonlexical parallel: the section says its named root ك ب د differs from this root, but both stage purposeful toil; “كَادِحٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ كَدْحًا” directs exertion toward meeting God. | terra: Every human is laboring laboriously toward the Lord and will meet Him, turning unavoidable toil into directed travel with an encounter at its end.
terra: Receiving the record in the right hand opens the successful outcome after every person's labor toward the Lord in 84:6.
terra: The right-hand traveler receives an easy reckoning, joining exertion on the way to ease at the end.
terra: Joyful return to one's people gives the successful laborer a reached homecoming.
terra: Receiving the record behind the back opens the opposed outcome and gives retreating bodily orientation to it.
terra: The failed traveler calls for destruction when confronted with his result.
terra: He enters a blazing fire, supplying the terminal destination of the backward-oriented branch.
terra: God creates and proportionately fashions, providing the making of a creature fit for the route before guidance is mentioned.
terra: God measures and then guides, joining creaturely fitting and direction in the same sequence as created humanity and the shown ridges.
terra: People prefer the nearer life, naming the choice of immediate ease that can block the harder saving course.
terra: The Hereafter is declared better and more lasting, giving the preferred near life its true comparison and end.

luna: The section’s pass is expressed in aid to the vulnerable; this ayah condemns failing to honor the orphan, a direct reversal of the care that marks the good route. | terra: Failure to honor the orphan is one concrete refusal of the pass's demand.

luna: The section’s route includes feeding on a hungry day; “وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ” condemns the opposite social act. | terra: Failure to urge one another to feed the poor reverses both feeding and the mutual moral counsel of the travelers.

luna: Against the section’s giving toward need, this ayah depicts consuming inheritance “أَكْلًا لَّمًّا,” an image of taking wealth in rather than using it for others. | terra: Devouring inheritance greedily shows wealth moving into consumption rather than outward through the pass.

luna: The section separates meaningful giving from a boast about heaps of property; “تُحِبُّونَ الْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا” names attachment to wealth as a contrary orientation. | terra: An excessive love of wealth identifies the attachment behind the refusals in 89:17-19.

luna: The section treats the two ridges as opposed ways of response; “فُجُورَهَا وَتَقْوَاهَا” gives the soul the corresponding paired moral alternatives. | terra: God inspires the soul with both its depravity and its wariness, restating the two disclosed moral directions without road vocabulary.

luna: After 91:8 names the soul’s opposing tendencies, this ayah says “قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن زَكَّاهَا,” identifying success with purifying the self rather than stopping at the fork. | terra: This ayah gives success as the end of one of the two possibilities named in 91:8: the one who purifies the soul succeeds.

luna: This completes the paired outcomes after 91:8–9: “وَقَدْ خَابَ مَن دَسَّاهَا” makes the failed course the contrary to self-purification. | terra: This ayah gives failure as the other end of 91:8, so the two shown possibilities culminate in two outcomes as they do in the section.

luna: The section’s two visible routes issue in divergent action; “إِنَّ سَعْيَكُمْ لَشَتَّىٰ” explicitly says human striving takes different courses. | terra: The declaration that human striving is diverse opens the same divided road scene: bodies are moving, but their exertions head in unlike directions.

luna: The section links the pass to costly, outward good; this branch begins “مَنْ أَعْطَىٰ وَاتَّقَىٰ,” giving and guarding oneself as one route. | terra: Giving and taqwa identify the active choice that 92:7 will ease toward ease, matching the costly acts that cross the pass.

luna: The section makes the hill a chosen response after guidance; this ayah adds the giver’s belief in “الْحُسْنَىٰ,” which underlies that trustful action. | terra: Affirming the best completes the disposition of the giver in 92:5 before that traveler is eased along the easier end.

luna: The section’s path demands effort, while this branch promises “لِلْيُسْرَىٰ” for the giver who believes and gives; it shows divine facilitation at the end of that course. | terra: God's promise to ease the giver toward ease makes moral action a road one is fitted to travel.
terra: Miserliness and imagined self-sufficiency identify the refusal corresponding to the man who will not undertake the pass.
terra: Denying the best completes the miser's stance before 92:10 names the difficult destination to which he is eased.
terra: Being eased toward hardship makes the avoided moral difficulty issue in another, ruinous difficulty.
terra: His wealth cannot help when he tumbles down; the downward fall and useless property answer the section's unmade ascent and consumed wealth.

luna: The section rules out lack of a guide as the reason for not starting; “إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا لَلْهُدَىٰ” states God’s responsibility for guidance within the same two-course passage. | terra: God states that guidance belongs to Him, confirming that the failure before the pass is not a failure to supply guidance.
terra: The blazing fire is warned as the far end of the withholding course described earlier in the surah.
terra: Entry into that fire is assigned to the most wretched, making the wrong course terminate in bodily arrival.
terra: Denial and turning away identify the refusal that carries the traveler to the fire of 92:14-15.
terra: The most wary person is kept distant from the fire, opening the opposite outcome to the denier who turned away.
terra: The person spared from fire gives wealth in order to purify himself, directly linking expenditure to the saving branch.
terra: Seeking the face of the Most High supplies the same Godward intention that accompanies patient spending in 13:22.
terra: Final satisfaction completes the outcome of the giver's course.

luna: The section insists that not taking the pass does not remove hardship; “مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا” places ease alongside it. | terra: God states that ease is present with hardship, directly qualifying what the difficult pass contains rather than promising a life without difficulty.

luna: This adjacent ayah repeats the ease-with-hardship promise, completing the passage’s insistence that hardship does not stand alone; its contribution is the reiterated assurance “إِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا.” | terra: The repeated assurance that ease accompanies hardship makes the relation emphatic and therefore contributes independently to the section's difficult-road scene.

luna: The section’s hand-turned millstone makes hardship a continuing exertion; after the ease promised in 94:5–6, this ayah says “فَإِذَا فَرَغْتَ فَانصَبْ,” directing the person to keep striving. | terra: When one task is finished, the addressee is commanded to rise into further exertion, turning received ease into purposeful new labor.

luna: This completes the exertion in 94:7 by directing it toward God: “وَإِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ فَارْغَب,” giving the climb its orientation. | terra: The exertion of 94:7 is given an upward destination by directing longing toward the Lord.
terra: The human is created in the finest stature, establishing the bodily height from which the two outcomes that follow diverge.
terra: The human is then returned to the lowest of the low, a vertical reversal of the possible ascent.
terra: Faith and good action are excepted from that descent and receive an unending reward.

luna: A branch of the section’s root ب ل د describes a horse lagging behind the frontrunners; this oath opens with horses charging and panting, giving the forward-moving scene against which that laggard is defined.

luna: The section’s dictionary branches define ك ب د as entering the middle and ق ح م as plunging into the center of a fearful severity; this ayah’s charging horses reach “فَوَسَطْنَ بِهِ جَمْعًا,” a concrete image of penetration into the middle.
terra: Heavy scales open the successful branch of the final two-way outcome.
terra: A pleasing life is the reached end for the person whose scales are heavy.
terra: Light scales open the opposite branch and immediately precede the downward destination in 101:9.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss of ق ح م includes falling from high to low; after the weighing in this surah, “فَأُمُّهُ هَاوِيَةٌ” makes the failed end a downward plunge. | terra: The person with light scales has an abyss as his destination; its هَاوِيَةٌ uses the falling root found in the dictionary definition of blind plunging.
luna: After 101:9 calls the fallen person’s end “هَاوِيَةٌ,” this question asks what that abyss is; its role is to open the answer supplied by 101:11.

luna: This is the answer to 101:10’s question about the downward end in 101:9: “نَارٌ حَامِيَةٌ” identifies the abyss as a blazing Fire. | terra: The neighbour identifies the abyss of 101:9 as a fiercely hot fire, completing the source section's fall-to-fire relation.
terra: Competitive accumulation distracts people, identifying wealth itself as the force that diverts them from the costly good.
terra: The distraction persists until the accumulators reach the graves, abruptly placing hoarded increase against the journey's end.
terra: Mutual counsel to truth and mutual counsel to patience exactly parallels the travelers' reciprocal counsel at the pass.

luna: The section presents feeding on a day of hunger; this ayah says God “أَطْعَمَهُم مِّن جُوعٍ” and secured Quraysh from fear, turning the scene around to show the divine provision that human feeding answers. | terra: God's feeding against hunger states the provision that the travelers themselves are required to mediate on a day of hunger.
terra: Denial of recompense introduces the person whose treatment of the vulnerable displays refusal of the road and its end.

luna: This ayah’s “يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ” (repelling the orphan) reverses the section’s route of mercy toward the orphan. | terra: Driving away the orphan is the direct opposite of the pass's care for the nearby orphan.

luna: The section feeds the hungry and needy; “وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ” gives the direct contrary, failure even to urge that food be given. | terra: Not urging the feeding of the poor reverses both the act and the reciprocal urging found in the section.
terra: Withholding even small assistance condenses the bodily non-action behind refusal of the pass.
